title: Design a news feed
dek: Open Zotato Snaps and the home screen shows new posts from the diners and restaurants you follow, newest first. Build it so it opens instantly, even when a food blogger with 50 lakh followers posts at dinner time.

items: Two ways to build a feed: gather posts from everyone you follow when you open the app (pull), or drop each new post into every follower's feed when it's posted (push).
Pull is cheap to write and slow to read; push is fast to read and expensive to write. Feeds are read far more than posted to, so push is the default.
Push breaks for accounts with lakhs of followers: one post becomes lakhs of writes. Pull those few accounts at read time and merge them in.
Keep each person's feed as a short list of post ids (a few hundred) in memory; fetch the posts themselves from a cache when showing them.
Don't build feeds for people who haven't opened the app in weeks. Build theirs when they come back.
Show the home feed: posts from accounts I follow, newest first, page by page.
A new post appears in followers' feeds within a few seconds.
Follow and unfollow; deleted posts disappear from feeds.
Out of scope here: ranking by interest (we'll note where it plugs in), ads, and comments.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: The first page of the feed in under 200 ms
New posts show within a few seconds; a minute for very big accounts is fine
The feed always opens, even if it's a little behind
1 crore people open the app daily; 20 lakh posts a day

items: Reads: 1 crore people × 5 opens is 5 crore feed reads a day, about 600 a second and 3,000 at dinner.
Posts: 20 lakh a day is about 23 a second.
Fan-out: if a post goes to 200 followers on average, that's 40 crore feed inserts a day, about 4,600 a second. Fine for a cluster of Redis machines.
The outlier: a food blogger with 50 lakh followers. One post means 50 lakh inserts; at 50,000 a second that's 100 seconds before the last follower sees it, and it competes with everyone else's posts.
Feed size: 500 post ids × 8 bytes for 1 crore active people is about 40 GB of ids, a few times that in Redis. Fits in memory across a handful of machines.
Post: `id` (sortable by time), `author_id`, `text`, `photos`, `created_at`, `deleted`.
Follow: `follower_id`, `followee_id`, `created_at`. Stored both ways, so "who do I follow" and "who follows me" are each one lookup.
Feed: per person, a list of `post_id`s newest first, capped at about 500.

body.label: API
body.say: Get the feed a page at a time with a cursor. Create a post. Follow or unfollow an account.

body.cap: Posting writes the post and puts a message on a queue. Fan-out workers look up the author's followers and add the post id to each one's feed list in Redis. Opening the app reads one list and fetches the posts from a cache.

body.x: Posting stays fast because the fan-out happens after: the post is saved, the author sees it at once, and workers spread it to followers' lists over the next seconds. Reading is one lookup for a list of ids, then one batch fetch of the posts, most of them from a cache.

body.name: First try
body.what: When someone opens the app, fetch the latest posts of everyone they follow and merge them by time.
body.use: Posting is one write, and the feed is always exactly up to date.
body.avoid: Following 200 accounts means 200 lookups and a merge on every open, 3,000 times a second at dinner. The feed is slow, and the database does it again on every refresh.
body.ex: A diner following 300 accounts waits a second or more every time they open the app.
body.like: Visiting every friend's house to ask what's new, every time you want news.

body.name: Better
body.what: When someone posts, add the post id to each follower's feed list. Reading is one list lookup.
body.use: Feeds open instantly, and the work happens once per post instead of once per read.
body.avoid: A post from an account with 50 lakh followers means 50 lakh writes, and most of those feeds belong to people who won't open the app today.
body.ex: A food blogger posts a biryani review at 8 pm; the fan-out queue backs up and everyone's posts arrive a minute late.
body.like: Each friend posting a letter to everyone they know. Fine for most people, a lot of stamps for a celebrity.

body.name: Best
body.kind: PUSH, BUT PULL THE BIG ACCOUNTS
body.what: Push posts from ordinary accounts. Mark accounts with more than about a lakh followers as big, skip fan-out for them, and pull their latest posts when a follower opens the feed, merging them into the list.
body.use: Fan-out stays small and steady, and reading adds only a few extra lookups (people follow few big accounts).
body.avoid: Two paths to keep correct, and the threshold needs tuning. Merging must keep the order right and drop duplicates.
body.ex: Your feed list has posts from 180 friends; at read time it merges in the latest from the 4 big restaurants and 1 blogger you follow.
body.like: Friends send you letters; for the newspaper, you pick it up yourself.

body.cap: Opening the feed: the posts pushed into your list from ordinary accounts, plus the latest posts pulled from the few big accounts you follow, merged by time. Fan-out never has to write 50 lakh lists for one post.

items: Cap each list at about 500 ids. Nobody scrolls further, and older pages can fall back to pulling.
Skip fan-out for people who haven't opened the app in, say, 30 days. When they come back, build their list by pulling once.
Deleted posts and unfollowed accounts: filter them out when reading, and clean the lists in the background. Never make a delete wait for 50 lakh list updates.
A new follow: add that account's last few posts to your list right away, so the feed changes when you expect it to.
Your own post goes into your own list at once, before the fan-out runs. Otherwise you open your feed, don't see it, and post it again.

Post ids that sort by time (time first, then a random part) make "newest first" a simple sort. The cursor is a position (time, then post id) of the last post seen, which works the same for pushed and pulled posts after merging.
New posts arriving while you scroll don't shift your page, because the cursor says where you were, not a page number.
Ranking by interest fits in later: take the first few hundred candidates from the list and score them. The list is still the source of candidates.
Fan-out workers behind: the queue holds the work; feeds are a few seconds or minutes late, never wrong.
A Redis machine lost: its users' lists are rebuilt by pulling, a little slower for a while.
Post cache down: fetch posts from the database in batches; slower, still works.
Junior / mid: pull versus push and why reads matter more, a feed list per user, a cache for posts, cursor pages.
Senior: the fan-out numbers, the celebrity problem and the hybrid, skipping inactive users, deletes filtered at read.
Lead: the threshold and two code paths, rebuild after loss, where ranking plugs in, and how fresh is fresh enough.
"Someone follows 5,000 accounts." Their list fills faster and turns over sooner, which is fine; cap how many big accounts are pulled per read.
"A big account drops below the threshold." Switch it back to push for new posts, and add its last few posts to followers' lists once, so they don't vanish from feeds.
"Show 'X liked this'?" That's a different kind of event fanned out the same way, with stricter limits so feeds aren't flooded.
"How fresh is fresh?" Seconds for ordinary accounts; for big accounts, the pull is exactly fresh, but cache it per account for a few seconds.
"How do you test it?" Seed a graph with ordinary and big accounts, post from each, and check order, duplicates and how long each feed took to update.

body.x: A feed is read far more than it's written. The read-heavy challenge shows the same lesson: a cache in front keeps the database calm.

practice.brief: Each test sends feed loads and posts. A feed load makes 3 queries (the feed list and the posts); feeds kept in a cache answer 95% of them; 10% of queries are writes (new posts fanned out to feeds). Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 1,500 requests a second: feed loads, posts and follows.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of feed loads succeed
Opening the app reads a feed that was put together before the user asked
At least 99.9% of feed loads succeed

tests.name: A food blogger posts
tests.desc: At 8 pm a blogger with 50 lakh followers posts, and they all open the app: 12,000 requests a second for 15 minutes.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of feed loads succeed

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (3,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of feed loads still succeed
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of feed loads still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (1,500 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of feed loads succeed

fr.label: Home feed: posts from people I follow, newest first
New posts appear in followers' feeds quickly

est.label: Feed loads a second at peak

decisions.q: Someone posts. When are their followers' feeds updated?
options: Only when each follower opens the app (merge everyone they follow then)
Push to followers' feeds at post time for most people; for accounts with millions of followers, merge their posts in when a feed is read
Push to every follower at post time, whoever posts
decisions.why: Pushing makes reads one lookup, but a celebrity post would mean millions of writes at once. Pulling just those few accounts at read time keeps both sides cheap.

decisions.q: What is stored in a feed list?
options: Full copies of each post with text and images
Post ids only; the posts are fetched (and cached) separately
decisions.why: Ids keep each feed small; an edited or deleted post changes in one place instead of in every follower's copy.

decisions.q: How does the app page through the feed?
options: Send the whole feed at once
A cursor: "posts older than this id"
decisions.why: New posts arrive at the top all the time, so page numbers shift and show repeats or skip posts. A cursor always continues from the last post seen.

hints.x: Reading the feed, posting, following. Which is most frequent, and how fresh must a feed be?
Posts are few (23 a second), but each one goes to ~200 followers. Work out the fan-out rate.
GET the feed with a cursor; POST a post; PUT or DELETE a follow.
Build each person's feed ahead of time (fan-out on write) and keep it in a cache, so a feed load is one fast read.
With feeds cached, 95% of queries never reach the database. The blogger spike quadruples traffic; size servers for it.
Two server groups and a Multi-AZ database so the feed always opens.

wrong.name: No cache
wrong.why: Every read goes to the database, which can't take the peak.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.
